mechanismLines: Asked at the market, the stallholders say the town's grain store is full of grain they would rather have sold.
A tavern keeper holds that a guest who falls ill is nursed by the inn servants, since the town keeps no house for the sick.
A guild factor reckons the store a stranger takes for provision was filled by the trades and is not theirs to open.
A clerk of the court says a man too ill to stand before it is left at the church, and the court's business waits on the parish.
samePageLines: Against ordinary trouble the town is ready, and against more than that it is not.
The streets here stay quiet, and the watch is not the reason.
Nothing that is run outside the law in Spitzplatz reaches inside the hall.
Keeping the town walls sound takes everything the town can spare.

17. (spine) The town walls around Spitzplatz are sound, and the muster that mans them is thinning. It is the kind of shortfall a town is slow to notice.
18. (spine) An interruption on the roads to Spitzplatz never reaches the table, and the granary is why, not the roads.
notes: Interpretive rule I adopted as the second reader, stated so it can be vetoed: I treated the ENTIRE printed file as 'the facts below' for questions 1-6 — THE TOWN card, THE STATE, the per-pool 'which reads:' typed fields, AND the machine lines printed under THE PAGE. Note the card itself seats 'anyone in the town' and 'every household here' as PUBLIC roster roles, which is the file's own evidence that a bare universal is not per se a quantity claim.

The judge labels every tier-1 drop 'T1-CERTAINTY' regardless of which of the seven questions actually fired. That label is not a measurement of the certainty arm — it is the arm name the judge prints for the whole tier-1 gate. Six faces were offered on that pool and five of the six (lines 3,4,5,6,8 — and 7) fire at least one arm; only the spine survives on its own merits and it ships nothing.

The single WITHHELD, WALL-5 on the walls pool, came from the judge's own page arms, not from me: I answered line 13 all-no. The badge reads 'readiness: Well-Defended' while the pool the writer was handed is 'readiness ADEQUATE'. mechanismLines: The market carries the town's own goods and goods brought in from elsewhere on the same stalls. Nothing marks which is which.
Something is always going out of the town. When one trade goes quiet, another does not.
Caravaneer's post stands, and the supply it depends on has failed further off. The building is kept and the skill is kept, and no goods come in.

Unlicensed trade goes on here and nothing is organised behind it… the odd part, in a town with a market and a road through it. What holds it small is nowhere written down, and whoever reads this next would do well to find out.

For magic the town has an alchemist's shop and no more, and whatever it wants past that comes from outside.

What stands to change hands between The Governing Council and The Order of the Watch is political influence, and the two are careful with each other.

Rule in the town runs through rooms, and each room has an officer who answers for it.

Prices in the town stay steady, and that steadiness does not depend only on the last thing that sold.
No standing arrangement for magic exists here, and what is wanted of it comes from outside.

What the town cannot grow, the road brings, and the town could not do without it.
One tie matters to the town more than the rest, and that shows in what the town does for it and what it withholds from everyone else.
Everyone here is tied to everyone else the ordinary way, by work, family, and proximity.

mechanismLines: A man on one of the gates says a stranger pays the gate. What the gate owes the hall is settled between the two of them, in the gate's own time.
A woman who keeps the hall books holds that a stranger who has paid at the gate has paid the town, whatever the men at the gate tell him.
A clerk of one of the courts says anyone who paid the toll may argue it in court, a stranger as readily as a carter.
One of the watch says what turns up after dark is dealt with after dark, there being nowhere to leave a man until morning.
A bailiff says the court hears in daylight what the watch settled in the dark, and nobody asks the court first.
A clerk in the hall reckons the purse does not run to a room to hold men in and never has. He does not say who asked for one.
A stallholder says a short weight goes to the court and comes back as a sum to pay, and the scales it was weighed on stay where they are.
The guild master says a sum paid out of a man's takings is forgotten, and the mark it leaves on his work is not.
A carter at one of the taverns reckons a man with a house here pays the sum and stays, and a man without one is told to go.
A gatekeeper says the men on the gates are handed a man and a direction and no reason for either.
A serjeant of the garrison holds that what comes at the town is the garrison's business and the men walked out of the gates are not.
One of the aldermen says the hall asks the trades for no more than the trades can carry.
A warden of one of the guilds says the carrying is the trades' and the asking is not.
The guilds' account is the likelier of the two, the hall having a purse to defend and the trades only a bill to pay.
Whoever keeps the toll book says a cart bound for the grain store is not kept waiting, whatever else is.
A potboy of the district says the watch is a trade that drinks on what it is owed.
A man who draws the wage holds that a town able to feed itself through a crisis and unable to pay him in full has decided something it has not said.
At the markets the people who deal there say the hall is settled with before anybody settles anything of their own.
A canon holds that the town keeps its word to the dead before it keeps its word to the living.
Grain is hard to keep in this town, the stallholders say, for anybody without a door of their own to keep it behind.
A journeyman reckons what a stranger takes for plenty is a store the trades filled and cannot open.
Some of the soldiers here are hired and the town knows which ones. The men out of the mercenary quarter are counted differently from the garrison, and counted openly.
A stranger is measured at the gate in a way he cannot name, and nobody there tells him what was done.
The city walls and gates stand better than the watch that should be on them. The keeping of the stone is met and the wage on the wall comes short.
samePageLines: The town holds its own ways in. The walls and gates settle where anything arrives and nothing about what it brings.
